route.central_idea: Before the phone, the inbox, or anyone else gets a piece of you, there are five minutes that are only yours — marked by the pour.
route.emotional_promise: Quiet self-possession: the felt relief of claiming a few minutes before the day starts claiming them for you.
route.product_role: The Solace dripper is the literal boundary object. The film's one deliberate action — setting the phone face-down and reaching for the dripper instead — makes the product the mechanism of the choice, not a backdrop to it. It stays in frame through the pour, the bloom, and the final held mug, closing on an unhurried, fully lit shot of the dripper itself on the counter.
route.visual_language: Quiet and continuous, no contrast-cutting: warm low window light, muted stoneware palette (terracotta, cream, soft grey), handheld-but-steady camera, close but not macro. Sound carries more of the emotion than music — water, steam, ceramic set down, a phone buzzing once, off-screen and ignored.
route.execution_example: 15s / 9:16 (D01): Open tight on a phone screen lighting up on a counter; a hand turns it face-down without looking. Cut to the same hand lifting the Solace dripper, setting it on a mug, spooning grounds. Slow spiral pour, water blooming the grounds in close-up (2-3s held). Cut to the person at a window, mug in both hands, steam rising, a single distant notification sound goes unanswered. Final beat (2s): dripper alone on the counter in soft full light, product fully legible, with an illustrative closing line such as 'Made in small batches' (exact copy owned by copywriter). The two 4:5 stills (D02) pull directly from this beat structure: still 1 = the pour/bloom close-up with the dripper as clear hero object; still 2 = the closing counter shot, product fully visible and legible, doubling as a clean DTC-linkable product image.

beats.picture: No cut. The camera follows the same hand past the phone to the dish rack by the sink. It lifts the terracotta Solace dripper out from between a pot lid and two forks. beats.vo: Your inbox had all night. It can wait out the bloom.

decisions.choice: No face appears anywhere in the film or stills. The person exists as a hand, grey cuffs and an off-screen sip.
decisions.reason: Hands doing specific tasks read as real, and a face here would add nothing a performance earns. It also keeps the viewer in the first person of the choice.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Hands before faces.' Craft brief: stock-lifestyle picture is rejected.

decisions.choice: The phone's lock screen reads '7:55' with a banner 'Standup moved to 8:00'. The B2 card 'Five minutes nobody else booked.' pays it off.
decisions.reason: The story has to read with the sound off. The time on screen does the five-minute arithmetic for the viewer, and the card turns the key message into calendar language this audience lives in.
decisions.source: Craft brief: 'Most vertical video plays with the sound off.' Brief key message: 'A five-minute ritual that slows your morning down, on purpose.'

decisions.choice: 'Five minutes' is always framed as the person's unbooked time, never as brew time.
decisions.reason: Brew time is not a verified fact. Tying five minutes to the calendar rather than the dripper keeps the key message without implying a performance claim.
decisions.source: Craft brief: Claims rule. Brief must-avoid: 'Unsupported performance claims.'

decisions.choice: One VO line only, 10 words ('Your inbox had all night. It can wait out the bloom.'). It sits on the bloom, right after the ignored buzz, with no VO in the hook or the product hold.
decisions.reason: The line adds the turn the picture can't: the day can wait. 'Bloom' ties it to pour-over, so it wouldn't work over another brand's footage. It carries no information the sound-off viewer needs. At 10 words in 4.5s it reads at about 2.2 words per second.
decisions.source: Craft brief: timing budget, and 'If a line would still make sense over any brand's footage, it is not finished.' Taste notes: 'Restraint over explanation,' 'Dry over sentimental.'

decisions.choice: The second, ignored buzz is shown as well as heard: the face-down phone shivers at the frame edge and light leaks from under it.
decisions.reason: The ignored interruption is the turn of the story. If it were sound only, sound-off viewers would miss it.
decisions.source: Craft brief: the story must read from picture and on-screen text alone.

decisions.choice: Hand-glazing is shown before it is stated: the uneven glaze line pooled at the foot is in close-up during the hold, and only then does the card say 'Hand-glazed stoneware.'
decisions.reason: Demonstrating a verified fact beats asserting it, and the adjective has something filmable behind it.
decisions.source: Craft brief: 'If an adjective survives, something filmable must back it up'; the skillet example demonstrates pre-seasoning rather than asserting it.

decisions.choice: The dripper comes off a dish rack beside the sink, next to a charging cable, and each scene gets one specific detail: cracked phone corner, 10K race mug, scuffed kitchen scale, frayed cuffs, stained drain hole.
decisions.reason: It grounds the ritual in a real weekday kitchen rather than a spotless set, and it avoids the brief's 'generic luxury imagery without a story.'
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Real kitchens have a dish rack and a charging cable' and 'One real detail per scene.'

decisions.choice: 'Dishwasher safe' stays out of the film and appears only in the still 2 subline.
decisions.reason: In the film it would bring in a second idea (convenience) against a story about choosing slow. On a product still aimed at add-to-cart it is a useful purchase fact.
decisions.source: Craft brief: 'One idea per spot.'

decisions.choice: The pour is filmed in real time. 'Slow' describes the pour speed, not the frame rate.
decisions.reason: Slow motion would make the dripper look expensive instead of used.
decisions.source: Taste notes, what we reject: 'Slow motion used to make something look expensive.'

decisions.choice: No music at all, not even late. The film ends on a kettle ticking as it cools, then room tone.
decisions.reason: The scene's real sounds carry the calm. A music bed would tell the viewer how to feel.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Sound design before music... Music comes in late, if at all.' Route visual language: sound carries more than music.

decisions.choice: The ending is a 2.0s clean product hold with the facts card in the top third, then a 2.0s CTA card on the same locked frame. There is no separate end card.
decisions.reason: The product is held longer than the 1.5s minimum before the CTA, and it never leaves the frame. Text is placed in negative space, never over the dripper.
decisions.source: Craft brief: product-moment rule and 'never over the product.' Taste notes reject a logo-on-color ending with no product.

decisions.choice: The CTA is 'Shop the Solace dripper: link in bio.' A colon is used instead of a dash.
decisions.reason: It is a specific verb plus a destination and serves the DTC site-visit objective. The colon keeps the card at 7 words even if a dash would be counted as a word.
decisions.source: Craft brief: CTA rule and the 7-words-per-card limit.

decisions.choice: Still 2's headline is 'The phone can have you now.', with the face-down phone kept soft in frame.
decisions.reason: It closes the film's logic with a dry edge: the five minutes are over and the day gets its turn. The phone strip can be cropped off for a clean product-page image.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Dry over sentimental.' Route: still 2 doubles as a DTC-linkable product image.

decisions.reason: At a calm 2.5 words per second it finishes 0.4s before the B4 lift and knock. 'Bloom' ties it to pour-over, so it wouldn't work over another brand's footage. It adds the turn the picture can't say and carries nothing a sound-off viewer needs.
decisions.source: Craft brief: 'A calm voiceover reads at about 2.5 words per second' and 'If a line would still make sense over any brand's footage, it is not finished.' Taste notes: 'Restraint over explanation,' 'Dry over sentimental.' Creative director's note N3.

decisions.choice: The ignored buzz in B3 is shown as well as heard: the face-down phone shivers at the edge of frame and light leaks from under it.
decisions.reason: The ignored interruption is the turn of the story. If it were sound only, sound-off viewers would miss it.
decisions.source: Craft brief: the story must read from picture and on-screen text alone.

decisions.choice: In the hero frame the used filter stays in, trimmed on set to sit a finger-width below the rim, and the lens is at rim height. The steam in B6 rises from the used grounds above the rim. The drain-hole stain is gone.
decisions.reason: The camera can't see the drain hole when the dripper stands on the counter, and a folded filter sticking up above the rim would change the silhouette in the one shot that has to be legible. B4 has no time to take the filter out, so it stays in, sitting low.
decisions.source: Craft brief: 'The product moment: the product is fully legible' and 'Write the picture.' Brief must-include: 'A readable closing product moment.' Creative director's notes N2 and N5.

decisions.choice: The hero frame has one real detail, the uneven glaze line pooling toward the foot. The 'Solace stamp' and the wet mug ring from the last draft are cut.
decisions.reason: The glaze line is true to the product and backs up the 'Hand-glazed stoneware' card on screen at the same moment. A maker's stamp isn't among the verified product details, so describing one risks showing a feature the product may not have. The ring couldn't exist anyway, because the mug sat on the scale, not on the wood.
decisions.source: Craft brief: 'If an adjective survives, something filmable must back it up.' Taste notes: 'One real detail per scene.' Creative director's note N2.

decisions.choice: Each scene gets one specific detail: the cracked phone corner in B1, the 10K race mug in B2, the ignored buzz in B3, the frayed cuffs in B4 and the glaze line in B5-B6. The dish rack and charging cable are set dressing, sharp in B2 and soft in B5.
decisions.reason: It grounds the ritual in a real weekday kitchen rather than a spotless set, and it avoids the brief's 'generic luxury imagery without a story'.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Real kitchens have a dish rack and a charging cable' and 'One real detail per scene.'

decisions.choice: 'Dishwasher safe' stays out of the film and appears only in the S2 subline.
decisions.reason: In the film it would bring in a second idea (convenience) against a story about choosing slow. On a product still aimed at add-to-carts it's a useful purchase fact.
decisions.source: Craft brief: 'One idea per spot.'

decisions.choice: The pour is filmed in real time. 'Slow' describes how fast the water is poured, not the frame rate.
decisions.reason: Slow motion would make the dripper look expensive rather than used.
decisions.source: Taste notes, what we reject: 'Slow motion used to make something look expensive.'

decisions.choice: There's no music at all, not even late. The film ends on the kettle ticking as it cools, then room tone.
decisions.reason: The scene's real sounds carry the calm. A music bed would tell the viewer how to feel.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Sound design before music... Music comes in late, if at all.' Route visual language: sound carries more than music.

decisions.choice: The ending is a 2.0s clean product hold with the facts card in the top third, then 2.0s of the CTA card on the same locked frame. There's no separate end card.
decisions.reason: The product is held longer than the 1.5s minimum before the CTA and never leaves the frame. All text sits in negative space, never over the dripper.
decisions.source: Craft brief: the product-moment rule and 'never over the product.' Taste notes reject a logo-on-color ending with no product in frame.

decisions.choice: The film, S1 and S2 all use the same CTA: 'Shop the Solace dripper: link in bio.' It uses a colon, not a dash.
decisions.reason: It's a specific verb plus a destination and serves the DTC site-visit objective. The stills will probably stay up longest, so each one asks for the click in the same words. The colon keeps the card at 7 words.
decisions.source: Craft brief: the CTA rule and the 7-words-per-card limit. Brief objective: 'Drive DTC site visits and add-to-carts.' Creative director's note N5.

decisions.choice: The S2 headline is still 'The phone can have you now.' with the face-down phone soft in frame. A tighter crop without the headline gives a clean product-page image.
decisions.reason: The headline closes the film's logic with a dry edge: the five minutes are over and the day gets its turn. The crop lets the same frame double as a DTC product image.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Dry over sentimental.' Route: still 2 doubles as 'a clean DTC-linkable product image.'

decisions.choice: No taste note is broken on purpose in this revision. The only break is from the route's window beat, and it's made to follow the taste notes.
decisions.reason: The taste notes ask for any deliberate break to be named. Note also that, as the creative director pointed out, these taste notes are marked as placeholder examples rather than Lucas's own, so every choice above that rests on them is only as reliable as that file.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'How to use these notes.' Creative director's overall read.

deviations.what: The route's shot of the person at a window, mug in both hands with steam rising, is replaced by a hands-only beat at the counter: the dripper is set down and both hands carry the mug up out of frame.
deviations.why: Taste notes explicitly reject 'Anyone gazing out a window holding a mug' and prefer 'Hands before faces'. The craft brief rejects stock-lifestyle picture such as gazing out a window. The route's 'final held mug' is kept.

deviations.what: The single unanswered notification moves from the window beat to the pour, at 4.8s. It's also made visible (the face-down phone shivers in soft focus at frame left) instead of being only a distant off-screen sound.
deviations.why: It's the turn of the story, and the craft brief requires the story to read with the sound off. Putting it on the bloom also cues the one VO line.

deviations.what: The pour and bloom beat runs 4.5s instead of the example's 2 to 3s.
deviations.why: It carries the only VO line (9 words, 5.0–8.6s) at a calm 2.5 words per second with room to breathe, and it's the heart of the idea: the minutes marked by the pour.

deviations.what: The example's single 2s final beat with the line 'Made in small batches' becomes two beats on one locked frame: a 2.0s product hold with 'Hand-glazed stoneware. Made in small batches.', then 2.0s with the CTA card.
deviations.why: The craft brief requires the product to be held for at least 1.5s before the end card and requires a verb-plus-destination CTA. Neither fits in one 2s beat without covering the product or rushing the read.

deviations.what: The dripper enters by being lifted from a dish rack one reach behind the mug. Seating the filter happens off-screen: one cut at 3.4s jumps straight to the grounds going into a filter that's already seated. The example shows the hand lifting the dripper and spooning grounds with no rack.
deviations.why: Taste notes: 'Real kitchens have a dish rack and a charging cable' and 'One real detail per scene.' It shows the product as a tool before it becomes the hero, and taking the filter step out keeps the hand from hurrying (creative director's note N1).

deviations.what: The example's 'slow spiral pour' is specified as a slow pour filmed in real time, with no slow motion. The route's 'warm low window light' comes from camera left, with no window in frame.
deviations.why: Taste notes reject slow motion used to make things look expensive, and they reject window-gazing imagery. The light quality the route asks for is kept.

deviations.what: The route's closing shot of the 'dripper itself on the counter' is specified with the used filter left in, trimmed below the rim, and the lens at rim height.
deviations.why: The brief requires a readable closing product moment, and a filter sticking up above the rim would change the dripper's silhouette. This follows creative director's note N2 and doesn't change the route's product role.

notes.overall_read: This is a strong script and it's on-route. With the sound off it reads as one clear story: the phone gets flipped, the dripper comes out of the rack, the buzz gets ignored during the bloom, and the dripper is held clean at the end. It has one idea, the product works as a tool before it becomes the hero, it states only verified facts, uses none of the banned words, and every deviation from the route is argued from the brief or the taste notes. The problems are all in execution, not structure. Two beats go over their time budgets: B2 has too many actions for 3 seconds, and the B3 VO is mistimed. The hero frame includes details the camera can't see. The hook frame is overstuffed, and one still has no CTA. It needs one revision pass and then it can go to the director. Two things for whoever runs the approval. First, this review is not approval: sign-off happens at the pipeline's human approval gate, and the orchestrating session should show the user where that is. Second, the taste notes I'm citing are marked as placeholder examples, not Lucas's own, so the taste-based notes are only as reliable as that file.
keep: The hook action: a hand flips the buzzing phone face-down without pausing, and the buzz cuts dead as the glass meets the wood. It's a specific action, with no face and no logo.
The setup and payoff between the 7:55 / 'Standup moved to 8:00' banner and the card 'Five minutes nobody else booked.' The five minutes come from the story, not from a claim.
The dripper is lifted out of the dish rack, so the product is a tool in use before it becomes the hero.
The ignored buzz in B3 is visible: the phone shivers, light leaks from under it, and the spiral doesn't break. The turn reads with the sound off.

The only VO line, 'Your inbox had all night. It can wait out the bloom.' It's dry, it could only be about this product, and it doesn't restate the picture. Trim it for time, but keep 'wait out the bloom'.
The pour is in real time with no slow motion, and sound design carries the whole spot: forks in the rack, ceramic clink, the fizz of the bloom, the kettle ticking as it cools. No music, no sting.
Hands only, with no face and no window. This replaces the route's window beat and is correctly logged as a deviation.

The locked closing frame: the product is uncovered for 4 seconds, all cards sit in the top third clear of the dripper, the facts card uses only verified facts, the CTA is a verb plus a destination, and there's no logo card.
The S2 headline 'The phone can have you now.' It's dry and knowing, and it's the other side of the central idea.

notes.note: B2 (1.5–4.5s) asks for six actions in 3.0s, in one unbroken real-time move: go to the rack, pull the dripper out from between the pot lid and forks, get back to a mug on a scale, set it down, seat a filter, and scoop in grounds. The only way to fit that is for the hand to hurry. Don't speed it up; take steps out. Keep the lift from the rack and the clink on the mug rim. Either have the filter already seated, or allow one cut (the route's example has one) that jumps straight to the grounds going in. Also write down where the mug and scale sit in relation to the phone. B3 needs the phone at frame left in a close vertical frame, and B5 needs it soft behind the dripper, so the layout of the counter has to be fixed in this beat.
notes.reason: A hurried hand in the setup beat says the opposite of 'slows your morning down', and the director can't shoot it as written without speeding it up.
notes.source: Craft brief: 'Timing is a budget, not a suggestion' and 'Write the picture' (who or what, doing what, where). Brief: tone 'quiet, warm, tactile'; key message 'A five-minute ritual that slows your morning down, on purpose.'

notes.note: Two things in the hero frame can't be filmed as written. (1) When the dripper stands on the counter, the drain hole is underneath it. The camera can't see 'a coffee stain in the drain hole', and in B6 the steam can't rise from there either. Steam comes off the spent grounds at the top. (2) The script never says what's inside the dripper. After B4 it still holds a wet paper filter full of spent grounds, and a folded filter sticking up above the rim changes the dripper's silhouette in the one shot that has to show it clearly. Decide this on the page. My preference is filter in, sitting low, because B4 has no time to take it out, but you need to write how it sits so the rim and glaze line stay clear. Make the uneven glaze line this frame's one real detail. It's true to the product, and it backs up the 'Hand-glazed stoneware' card on screen at the same moment.
notes.reason: This is the closing product moment the brief requires. If the page leaves it open, it gets decided on set, and whatever is decided there also becomes the S2 still.
notes.source: Craft brief: 'Write the picture' (observable action) and 'The product moment: the product is fully legible.' Brief must-include: 'A readable closing product moment.' Taste notes: 'One real detail per scene.'

notes.note: The VO is cued to start after the buzz at about 4.8s, so the 11 words get about 4.1s, not the full 4.5s your deviation note used to get 2.2 words per second. At a calm 2.5 words per second the line ends around 9.3s, which runs over the dripper lift and ceramic knock in B4. Fix the timing without speeding up the read. Trim the line to about 9 words and keep 'wait out the bloom', or move the buzz as early as the pour allows. Either way the VO should end before 9.0s with some room to breathe.
notes.reason: As timed now, the spot's only VO line either gets read faster than calm or runs into the next beat's action and sound.
notes.source: Craft brief: 'A calm voiceover reads at about 2.5 words per second' and 'Every beat has a start and end time in seconds. Beats run back to back.'

notes.note: The action is right, but the frame is overstuffed. A tight shot on the phone can't also show a cable running to an outlet behind the dish rack. Meanwhile the viewer has 1.5s to read '7:55' and 'Standup moved to 8:00' before the phone gets flipped. That banner sets up 'Five minutes nobody else booked', so it's the one thing this frame has to get across. Make the cracked screen corner this scene's one real detail, and take the cable, outlet and dish rack out of this shot. They already appear soft in the background of B5. Write the timing so the screen is lit and readable from the first frame, and have the flip land at the end of the beat, not in the middle. Keep the banner to its current four words or fewer.
notes.reason: The sound-off story starts with that banner, and nothing on the page tells the director to give it time to be read ahead of the set dressing.
notes.source: Craft brief: 'Most vertical video plays with the sound off' (the story must read from picture and on-screen text alone) and 'The hook is a specific action in the first 1.5 seconds.' Taste notes: 'One real detail per scene.'

notes.note: D02-S2 inherits B5's problems, and they matter more here because this frame is meant to double as a clean product-page image. Drop the drain-hole stain: the camera can't see it, and on a product page a stain looks like a flaw. Specify the filter the same way you do in the B5 fix. D02-S1 has no call to action at all. Give its subline the same verb plus destination that the film and S2 use, and leave the headline as it is.
notes.reason: The stills will probably stay up longest on the DTC site and in the feed. One is described from a frame that can't be shot as written, and the other doesn't ask for the click the brief is paying for.
notes.source: Brief objective: 'Drive DTC site visits and add-to-carts.' Craft brief: 'The CTA is a specific verb plus a destination.' Approved route: still 2 'doubling as a clean DTC-linkable product image.'

responses.what_changed: B2 no longer has the hand walk to the sink or seat a filter on camera. It now has two actions in one continuous move: the lift from the dish rack (1.5–2.5s), then lowering the dripper onto the mug rim (2.5–3.4s, keeping the clink). One cut at 3.4s goes to a close shot of a spoon tipping grounds into a filter that's already seated (3.4–4.5s). The dish rack now stands one reach directly behind the mug, so nothing has to hurry. B2 also fixes the counter layout for the rest of the film. The mug on the scale sits mid-counter, the face-down phone one hand-width to its left (so it's at frame left in B3), the dish rack with the outlet and unplugged cable at the back, and the front strip of wood is left empty for the dripper in B4 and B5 (so the phone, rack and cable sit soft behind it in B5).

The drain-hole stain is cut from B5, and the steam in B6 now rises from the used grounds just above the rim. The filter stays in: in B2 it's trimmed on set to sit a finger-width below the rim, and B5 is shot with the lens at rim height, so the rim reads as one unbroken line and no paper or grounds show. The uneven glaze line pooling toward the foot is now the frame's one real detail, on screen at the same moment as the 'Hand-glazed stoneware' card. I also cut the 'Solace stamp' (not among the verified product details) and the wet mug ring (the mug sat on the scale, so it couldn't leave a ring on the wood).

The line is trimmed to 9 words, 'Email had all night. It can wait out the bloom.', keeping 'wait out the bloom'. The buzz stays at 4.8s, near the start of the pour, and the VO runs from 5.0s to about 8.6s at a calm 2.5 words per second, leaving 0.4s of pour and bloom before the B4 lift and knock at 9.0s. This also corrects my last draft, which counted the old line as 10 words and timed it across the full 4.5s. It was 11 words and had only about 4.1s after the buzz.

The cable, outlet and dish rack are out of B1. The shot looks almost straight down, so only the phone and bare wood are in frame, and the cracked screen corner is the frame's one real detail. The screen is lit and readable from the first frame, showing '7:55' and the four-word banner 'Standup moved to 8:00'. The hand doesn't enter until 0.9s, and the flip lands at 1.5s, at the end of the beat. The phone buzzes from frame one and the buzz still cuts dead as the glass meets the wood. The rack and cable now appear in the B2 layout and soft in the B5 background.

D02-S2 no longer mentions the drain-hole stain, and it specifies the filter exactly as B5 does: trimmed a finger-width below the rim, lens at rim height, rim unbroken, and no paper or grounds showing. The glaze line is its one detail. D02-S1 keeps its headline, and its subline now ends with the same CTA as the film: 'Shop the Solace dripper: link in bio.' S2's subline uses the same wording, so the film and both stills ask for the click identically.

judges.verdict: C wins, and it is the only script I would put in front of the client today. B and C are the same strong film. The picture carries the idea: a phone flipped at 7:55 before an 8:00 standup, a pour that doesn't break when the phone buzzes, hands only, a race mug, real kitchen clutter, and a dry VO line the picture can't say. C is the version a crew can actually shoot. It maps the counter layout, times the hook to the frame and adds one cut so beat 2 fits in 3 seconds. It also hides the used filter in the hero shot, which B leaves unsolved along with a coffee stain. Two small notes go with C's approval. Let the VO run to 9.0s so it reads calmly. If the product has a Solace stamp, turn it to camera in the closing shot. A doesn't ship: its picture and sound fields are blank, it keeps the window-and-mug shot the taste notes reject, it puts the key message on screen as a tagline, and it crams about 17 words onto a 2-second end card. On where you'd approve this: this review only gives a recommendation. The approval itself is yours, at the script approval gate in the studio pipeline where the run stops for you. That's where you'd sign off on C.

specificity.evidence: Every PICTURE and SOUND field reads '(not specified)'. The direction is stuffed into the VO field in brackets, and a production note ('No super. Keep the bloom clean.') sits in the ON-SCREEN field. The direction that is there is generic: 'an unbranded phone... generic notification UI', 'sets it on a mug and spoons in grounds', 'the talent at a window, mug in both hands'. It gives no location, props or real detail a crew could dress a set with.

distinctiveness.evidence: Apart from the end card ('Solace Ceramic Pour-Over / Hand-glazed stoneware. Made in small batches.'), any pour-over, kettle or coffee brand could run this unchanged. The phone face-down, the spiral pour and the mug at a window are category stock.

brief_fit.evidence: It delivers the central idea and the must-includes: the dripper as tool from 00:02, and a legible counter shot at 00:11-00:15. It uses only verified facts. But 00:08-00:11 is 'the talent at a window, mug in both hands, steam rising'. The taste notes reject that shot outright ('Anyone gazing out a window holding a mug'), and it pushes toward the brief's 'generic luxury imagery' must-avoid. It keeps the route's illustrative window beat without flagging the break.

craft.evidence: The hook works: 'a hand turns it face-down without looking' in 0-2s. Going with no VO is a defensible restraint choice, and the phone-glow cut-in for sound-off viewers is smart. But the cards explain rather than trust: 'First, five minutes that are only yours.' restates the central idea, and 'Slow your morning down. On purpose.' is the key message read out as a tagline. The 13-15s end card stacks a headline, the product name, two facts and a CTA button, about 17 words in 2s. That breaks the 7-words-per-card rule.

A.weakness: It is the route's illustrative example transcribed with captions added. It keeps the rejected window-and-mug shot, has no real detail in any scene, and puts the key message on screen instead of dramatizing it.

specificity.evidence: The props and sounds are strong: 'cracked screen corner', 'white charging cable loops back to an outlet behind the dish rack', 'Standup moved to 8:00', 'between a pot lid and two forks', a mug 'printed Riverside 10K 2019' on a 'scuffed black kitchen scale', 'Forks rattle in the rack'. It loses points on shootability. 1.5-4.5s is one continuous take ('No cut') in which the hand crosses to the rack, lifts the dripper, sets it on the mug, seats a filter and scoops grounds, and that doesn't fit in 3s. The counter layout is never fixed either.

distinctiveness.evidence: 'An uneven line of terracotta glaze pooled toward the foot' shows 'hand-glazed' instead of asserting it, and 'the Solace stamp turned to camera' ties the hero shot to this brand. The ritual itself (phone down, gooseneck spiral, bloom) is still category-generic, so a competitor could reuse most of beats 1-4.

brief_fit.evidence: The central idea lands in picture: the phone goes face-down, then buzzes during the pour and 'The spiral doesn't break.' The card 'Five minutes nobody else booked.' puts the proposition in the audience's calendar language. Facts are limited to 'Hand-glazed stoneware. Made in small batches.' It swaps the window shot for 'No face, no window' and 'No logo card, no colored background', both following the taste notes. The problem is the DTC hero: 'a coffee stain in the drain hole' and an unaddressed used filter in the closing product shot. A client selling a $38 dripper will push back on that.

craft.evidence: The hook is a specific action inside 1.5s: 'turns the phone face-down mid-buzz, without pausing.' The VO 'Your inbox had all night. It can wait out the bloom.' is dry and adds a turn the picture can't say. At 11 words from about 4.9s to 9.0s it runs about 2.7 wps, slightly quick. Sound-off holds: 'it shivers on the wood and a line of light leaks from under its edge'. The product holds for 4s across 11-15s, and cards sit 'in the top third, clear of the dripper'. It loses points for the physically impossible 3s continuous take, and it is unclear whether 9-11s into 11-13s is a cut.

B.weakness: The film is right but the page won't shoot as written. Beat 2 packs five actions into a single 3s take, and the closing hero shot has a used filter and a coffee stain the script never solves.

specificity.evidence: It keeps everything B has and adds blocking a crew can shoot. The counter is mapped once ('The face-down phone lies one hand-width to the mug's left. The dish rack stands directly behind the mug... one reach away'). Action is timed to the frame ('Nothing else moves until 0.9s... The flip lands at 1.5s', 'One cut at 3.4s'). The hero-shot problem gets a physical fix: 'top edge trimmed to sit a finger-width below the dripper's rim... the used grounds are out of sight at this height'.

distinctiveness.evidence: 'The terracotta glaze runs unevenly and pools into a thicker line toward the foot, catching the light' is named as the frame's one real detail and demonstrates 'hand-glazed'. B's 'Solace stamp turned to camera' is gone, though, so the brand name only appears in the CTA card. Beats 1-4 remain a ritual any ceramic-dripper brand could claim.

brief_fit.evidence: The central idea is carried entirely by picture: the flip, then 'At 4.8s the phone buzzes once... The spiral doesn't break.' The product is the mechanism of the choice, a tool at 1.5-9.0s and a hero at 11-15s. 'The Solace dripper stands alone and sharp... its full profile from rim to foot in frame.' Claims are limited to the two verified facts. Every taste note is honoured: hands only, no window, sound before music, no logo card.

craft.evidence: The hook is readable sound-off ('7:55 in large type', 'Standup moved to 8:00') and lands its action by 1.5s. Cards are 5, 6 and 7 words, each in the top third and clear of the product. The product is held and legible for the full 2.0s before the CTA card, then 2s more. Two things to fix. 'The VO runs from 5.0s to about 8.6s' gives 10 words 3.6s, about 2.8 wps, a bit quick for a calm read, so let it run to 9.0s. The filter is 'already seated' after the 3.4s cut when the dripper came out of the rack bare, a small continuity cheat to cover in the edit.

C.weakness: The closing product shot has no brand mark in frame. 'Solace' only reaches a sound-off viewer through the CTA card, so the dripper could read as any terracotta cone. The VO window is also 0.4s too short for a calm read.

judges.verdict: C is the one to approve, and it's the only one I could shoot tomorrow without calling anyone. The set is laid out like a floor plan, every action has a time, and the hero frame's lens height and light are given. It fixes each physical problem B has. C needs three on-set calls, and none changes the script: cut at 9.0s to cover the brew time, add a backlight so the steam shows, and use the platform shop button instead of 'link in bio' if it runs as paid. B is a looser version of the same film. Its 3-second one-take can't be done, and its closing frame needs a drain hole that faces the counter. A follows the route faithfully but isn't a shooting script: picture and sound read '(not specified)', and the beats are generic. On 'where would I approve this': this review only recommends which script to approve (C). Nothing in the prompt says where the pipeline's creative-director approval step is.

specificity.evidence: I could shoot this from the page. It sets the whole counter out like a floor plan: "a white mug printed 'Riverside 10K 2019' sits on a black kitchen scale... The face-down phone lies one hand-width to the mug's left. The dish rack stands directly behind the mug... The strip of wood between the scale and the front edge of the counter is left empty." Lens height is given ("lens level with the dripper's rim"), so is key-light direction ("from camera left"), and every action has a time ("The flip lands at 1.5s", "At 4.8s the phone buzzes once"). It even fixes a problem before we hit it: the filter is "trimmed to sit a finger-width below the dripper's rim", so the used grounds stay out of the hero shot. It loses a point because the 9.0s beat never says whether it's a cut. The pour is "filmed in real time" from 4.5s, then at 9.0s there's "one last drop". A real brew takes minutes, so the time jump has to be a cut, but the page doesn't say so. The filter also appears "already seated" in a dripper that was just lifted out of a dish rack, which is a continuity cheat I'd have to choose to live with.

distinctiveness.evidence: The lived-in details are specific to this film and work against luxury clichés: the cracked phone, the race mug, the "frayed grey cuffs", the calendar banner 'Standup moved to 8:00' at '7:55'. The card "Five minutes nobody else booked." is a line this campaign can own. The hero detail, "the terracotta glaze runs unevenly and pools into a thicker line toward the foot", ties the picture to the hand-glazed fact. Still, another brand of ceramic dripper could run it by swapping the name in the CTA. The story belongs to the category, not only to Solace.

brief_fit.evidence: It delivers the central idea. The phone goes face-down and the same hand goes straight to the dripper ("the hand reaches straight back into the rack and lifts the terracotta Solace dripper"), so the product is how the choice gets made. The VO "Email had all night. It can wait out the bloom." covers the inbox. Only verified facts appear on screen: "Hand-glazed stoneware. Made in small batches." The closing product moment is held for 4s. Two departures from the route aren't flagged: the buzz happens on screen rather than "off-screen", and there is "No face and no window". # Taste notes

> **EXAMPLE NOTES — written by Claude to test the taste mechanism, not Lucas's own.**
> Replace these with Lucas's real notes and references. Every agent treats this file as the
> studio's point of view, so the output will only be as specific as what's written here.

## What we like

- **Restraint over explanation.** If the picture already says it, the words stay quiet. The
  best spots trust the viewer to get it.
- **Hands before faces.** Show a face only when the performance earns it. Hands doing a
  specific task read as real; a smiling face reads as stock.
- **Sound design before music.** Real sounds from the scene (a pour, ceramic on wood, a
  kettle click) carry the mood. Music comes in late, if at all.
- **Dry over sentimental.** A line with a small, knowing edge beats a line that tells people
  how to feel.
- **The product is a tool, then a hero.** It's shown in use, doing its job, before it gets
  its clean product shot in the last seconds.
- **One real detail per scene** that only this place or person would have: a chipped mug, a
  sticky note on the fridge, a specific brand of kettle scale.

## What we reject

- Anyone gazing out a window holding a mug.
- Sun "flooding" a spotless kitchen. Real kitchens have a dish rack and a charging cable.
- A voiceover that sounds like a tagline being read aloud.
- Slow motion used to make something look expensive.
- Endings that fade to a logo on a colored background with no product in the frame.

## How to use these notes

Cite the specific note when a choice follows from it, and say so explicitly when you break
one on purpose and why.
